## Problem 1

### Description
```{r}
library(p8105.datasets)
data("ny_noaa")
ny_noaa

# Missing data
missing_sum =
  ny_noaa |>
  summarize(
    across(
      c(prcp, snow, snwd, tmax, tmin),
      ~sum(is.na(.x))
    )
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = everything(),
    names_to = "variable",
    values_to = "n_missing"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    pct_missing = 100 * n_missing / nrow(ny_noaa)
  )

missing_sum |>
  knitr::kable(
    digits = 2,
    col.names = c(
      "Variable",
      "Missing Values",
      "Percent Missing"
    )
  )
```
The `ny_noaa` dataset contains `r nrow(ny_noaa)` observations and `r ncol(ny_noaa)` variables from `r n_distinct(ny_noaa$id)` weather stations in New York State. Each row represents a daily weather observation at a particular station.

The variables include station ID (`id`), observation date (`date`), precipitation (`prcp`), snowfall (`snow`), snow depth (`snwd`), maximum temperature (`tmax`), and minimum temperature (`tmin`).

Missing values are major issue in this dataset, particularly for maximum and minimum temperatures, which both have approximately 43.71% missing observations. Snow depth also has considerable missingness (22.80%), while precipitation has the lowest percentage (5.62%). These missing values may affect the representativeness of the temperature and snowfall analyses, so they are excluded from the relevant calculations.

### Data Cleaning
```{r}
ny_noaa_clean =
  ny_noaa |>
  mutate(
    year = lubridate::year(date),
    month = lubridate::month(date),
    day = lubridate::day(date),
    tmax = as.numeric(tmax) / 10,
    tmin = as.numeric(tmin) / 10,
    prcp = prcp / 10
  )

ny_noaa_clean

```

### Commonly observed values
```{r}
snow_df =
  ny_noaa_clean |>
  filter(!is.na(snow)) |>
  count(snow, sort = TRUE) |>
  slice_head(n = 10)

snow_df |>
  knitr::kable(
    col.names = c(
      "Snowfall (mm)",
      "Number of Observations"
    )
  )
```
The most commonly observed snowfall value is 0 mm (2,008,508 observations), since most days have no measurable snowfall. Other common values include 25, 13, 51, and 76 mm, which correspond approximately to 1, 0.5, 2, and 3 inches. This suggests that snowfall may have originally been recorded in inches and converted to millimeters.

### Average max temperature in January and in July
```{r}
jan_jul_df =
  ny_noaa_clean |>
  filter(month %in% c(1, 7)) |>
  group_by(id, year, month) |>
  summarize(
    mean_tmax = mean(tmax, na.rm = TRUE),
    n_obs = sum(!is.na(tmax)),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  filter(n_obs > 0) |>
  mutate(
    month = factor(
      month,
      levels = c(1, 7),
      labels = c("January", "July")
    )
  )

jan_jul_df |>
  ggplot(
    aes(x = year, y = mean_tmax, group = id)
  ) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.15, color = "steelblue") +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.15, size = 0.5) +
  facet_grid(. ~ month) +
  labs(
    title = "Average Maximum Temperature by Station",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Average Maximum Temperature (°C)"
  )

jan_jul_df |>
  group_by(month) |>
  summarize(
    minimum = min(mean_tmax),
    maximum = max(mean_tmax),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 2)
```
The plot shows a clear seasonal difference, with average maximum temperatures generally ranging from -10°C to 10°C in January and 20°C to 35°C in July. January temperatures fluctuate more noticeably across years, while July temperatures remain relatively stable. There are also some unusual observations, such as a particularly low July temperature around 1988 and several extremely low January temperatures. Overall, there is no clear long-term increasing or decreasing trend, although temperature varies across stations and years.

### Two-panel plots
```{r fig.width=12, fig.height=10}
p_temp =
  ny_noaa_clean |>
  filter(!is.na(tmax), !is.na(tmin)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = tmin, y = tmax)) +
  geom_bin2d(bins = 50) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c() +
  labs(
    title = "Maximum vs Minimum Temperature",
    x = "Minimum Temperature (°C)",
    y = "Maximum Temperature (°C)",
    fill = "Count"
  )

p_snow =
  ny_noaa_clean |>
  filter(snow > 0, snow < 100) |>
  ggplot(
    aes(x = factor(year), y = snow)
  ) +
  geom_boxplot(
    fill = "lightblue",
    outlier.alpha = 0.2
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of Snowfall by Year",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Snowfall (mm)"
  ) +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(
      angle = 90,
      hjust = 1,
      size = 7
    )
  )

p_temp / p_snow
```

The histogram shows a strong positive relationship between minimum and maximum daily temperatures. Most observations are concentrated along an upward-sloping diagonal, indicating that higher minimum temperatures are generally associated with higher maximum temperatures. A few isolated observations show unusually high or low temperatures, potentially indicating extreme values or data quality issues that may require further investigation.

The snowfall distributions are relatively consistent across years, with median snowfall remaining around 25 mm and similar interquartile ranges. Most observations fall between approximately 13 and 51 mm, although larger snowfall amounts occur occasionally. A few years, particularly 1998, 2006, and 2010, show some high outliers. Overall, the plot suggests that the distribution of positive daily snowfall amounts below 100 mm remained fairly stable across the study period.

## Problem 2
```{r}
nhanes_covar =
  read_csv(
    "Data/nhanes_covar.csv",
    skip = 4,
    show_col_types = FALSE
  ) |>
  janitor::clean_names()

nhanes_accel =
  read_csv(
    "Data/nhanes_accel.csv",
    show_col_types = FALSE
  ) |>
  janitor::clean_names()

# exclude participants less than 21 years of age & missing demographic data
nhanes_covar =
  nhanes_covar |>
  filter(age >= 21) |>
  drop_na() |>
  mutate(
    sex = factor(
      sex,
      levels = c(1, 2),
      labels = c("Male", "Female")
    ),
    education = factor(
      education,
      levels = c(1, 2, 3),
      labels = c(
        "Less than high school",
        "High school equivalent",
        "More than high school"
      )
    )
  ) |>
  drop_na()

nhanes_df =
  inner_join(
    nhanes_covar,
    nhanes_accel,
    by = "seqn"
  )

nhanes_df |>
  select(seqn, age, sex, education) |>
  head(6) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

The cleaned and merged dataset contains `r nrow(nhanes_df)` participants and `r ncol(nhanes_df)` variables. Participants younger than 21 and those with missing demographic information were removed. Sex and education were converted to factors so that they could be presented with meaningful labels and ordered consistently in tables and visualizations. All original variables were retained in the merged dataset.

### Number of men and women by education levels
```{r}
education_table =
  nhanes_df |>
  count(education, sex) |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = sex,
    values_from = n,
    values_fill = 0
  )

# readable table
education_table |>
  knitr::kable(
    caption = "Number of Participants by Sex and Education Level"
  )

# visualization for age distribution of men and women by education levels
nhanes_df |>
  ggplot(aes(x = sex, y = age, fill = sex)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.7) +
  facet_wrap(~education, nrow = 1) +
  labs(
    title = "Age Distribution by Sex and Education",
    x = "Sex",
    y = "Age (years)",
    fill = "Sex"
  ) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

After excluding participants younger than 21 and those with missing demographic information, 228 participants remained. The group with more than a high school education had the most participants (115), followed by high school equivalent (58) and less than high school (55). Men and women were relatively evenly distributed overall, although the high school equivalent group had more men than women.

Participants with more than a high school education tended to be younger, with median ages around 41–44 years, compared with approximately 60–61 years for those with less than a high school education. In the high school equivalent group, women had a higher median age than men. Overall, age distributions varied more across education levels than between sexes.

### Total daily activity
```{r}
nhanes_df =
  nhanes_df |>
  mutate(
    total_activity = rowSums(
      across(starts_with("min")),
      na.rm = TRUE
      )
    )

nhanes_df |>
  select(seqn, age, sex, education, total_activity)

# Plot age vs total_activity
nhanes_df |>
  ggplot(
    aes(
      x = age,
      y = total_activity,
      color = sex
    )
  ) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~education, nrow = 1) +
  labs(
    title = "Total Daily Activity by Age",
    x = "Age (years)",
    y = "Total Daily Activity (MIMS)",
    color = "Sex"
  )

activity_age_summary =
  nhanes_df |>
  mutate(
    age_group = case_when(
      age < 40 ~ "21–39",
      age < 60 ~ "40–59",
      TRUE ~ "60+"
    )
  ) |>
  group_by(age_group) |>
  summarize(
    median_activity = median(total_activity, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

activity_age_summary |>
  knitr::kable(
    digits = 2,
    caption = "Median Daily Activity by Age Group"
  )
```

Total daily activity generally decreased with age, particularly among participants older than 60. The trend was more noticeable in the lower education groups, while participants with more than a high school education showed relatively stable activity levels through middle age. There was considerable individual variation, and differences between men and women were not consistent across education groups.

Median daily activity was similar for participants aged 21–39 (14,046.28 MIMS) and 40–59 (14,131.85 MIMS), but decreased to 10,417.80 MIMS among participants aged 60 or older. This suggests that older adults generally had lower daily physical activity, while younger and middle-aged participants had comparable activity levels.

### 24-hour activity time courses
```{r}
nhanes_long =
  nhanes_df |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = starts_with("min"),
    names_to = "minute",
    values_to = "mims"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    minute = as.numeric(
      str_remove(minute, "min")
    ) - 1
  )

# time summary
activity_time =
  nhanes_long |>
  group_by(education, sex, minute) |>
  summarize(
    mean_mims = mean(mims, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

activity_time

# Plots
activity_time |>
  ggplot(
    aes(
      x = minute,
      y = mean_mims,
      color = sex
    )
  ) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.3, linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_smooth(
    se = FALSE,
    span = 0.08,
    linewidth = 1
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~education, nrow = 1) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = seq(0, 1440, by = 360),
    labels = c(
      "12 AM", "6 AM", "12 PM", 
      "6 PM", "12 AM"
    ),
    limits = c(0, 1440)
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "24-Hour Activity Patterns",
    x = "Time of Day",
    y = "Mean Activity (MIMS)",
    color = "Sex"
  ) +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(
      angle = 45,
      hjust = 1
    )
  )
```

Activity levels are lowest during the early morning (around 4 AM), increase sharply after 6 AM, and remain relatively high throughout the day before declining at night. Women generally show higher daytime activity than men, particularly in the high school equivalent and more than high school education groups. In the less than high school group, activity patterns are more similar between sexes. Overall, all three education groups show similar daily activity cycles, but the magnitude and timing of activity peaks differ by sex and education level.

## Problem 3

Data import
```{r}
jan_2020 =
  read_csv(
    "Data/Jan 2020 Citi.csv",
    show_col_types = FALSE
  ) |>
  mutate(
    year = 2020,
    month = "January"
  )

jul_2020 =
  read_csv(
    "Data/July 2020 Citi.csv",
    show_col_types = FALSE
  ) |>
  mutate(
    year = 2020,
    month = "July"
  )

jan_2024 =
  read_csv(
    "Data/Jan 2024 Citi.csv",
    show_col_types = FALSE
  ) |>
  mutate(
    year = 2024,
    month = "January"
  )

jul_2024 =
  read_csv(
    "Data/July 2024 Citi.csv",
    show_col_types = FALSE
  ) |>
  mutate(
    year = 2024,
    month = "July"
  )

```

Combine data
```{r}
citibike =
  bind_rows(
    jan_2020,
    jul_2020,
    jan_2024,
    jul_2024
  ) |>
  mutate(
    month = factor(
      month,
      levels = c("January", "July")
    ),
    weekdays = factor(
      weekdays,
      levels = c(
        "Monday", "Tuesday", "Wednesday",
        "Thursday", "Friday", "Saturday", "Sunday"
      )
    ),
    member_casual = factor(
      member_casual,
      levels = c("casual", "member"),
      labels = c("Casual", "Member")
    ),
    rideable_type = factor(
      rideable_type,
      levels = c("classic_bike", "electric_bike"),
      labels = c("Classic", "Electric")
    )
  )

citibike
```

The combined dataset contains `r nrow(citibike)` rides and `r ncol(citibike)` variables. Each row represents one Citi Bike ride from the 1% sample of rides lasting less than four hours.

The dataset includes ride ID, bike type, day of the week, ride duration in minutes, starting and ending stations, membership status, year, and month.

There are some missing station names, but the ride duration and membership information are available for the observations used in the following analyses. Missing starting station names are excluded only when ranking the most popular starting stations.

### Number of rides by year, month, and membership

```{r}
ride_table =
  citibike |>
  group_by(year, month, member_casual) |>
  summarize(
    n_rides = n(),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = member_casual,
    values_from = n_rides
  ) |>
  arrange(year, month)

ride_table |>
  knitr::kable(
    caption = "Number of Citi Bike Rides by Year, Month, and Membership"
  )
```

The number of sampled Citi Bike rides increased substantially from 2020 to 2024, with July consistently having more rides than January. Members accounted for the majority of rides in all four months. July 2024 had the highest number of sampled rides, with 36,262 member rides and 10,894 casual rides. These patterns suggest greater cycling activity during warmer months and increased system usage over time.

### Five most popular starting stations in July 2024

```{r}
top_stations =
  citibike |>
  filter(
    year == 2024,
    month == "July",
    !is.na(start_station_name)
  ) |>
  count(
    start_station_name,
    sort = TRUE
  ) |>
  slice_head(n = 5)

top_stations |>
  knitr::kable(
    col.names = c(
      "Starting Station",
      "Number of Rides"
    ),
    caption = "Five Most Popular Starting Stations in July 2024"
  )
```

### Median ride duration by weekday, month, and year
```{r}
median_duration_df =
  citibike |>
  group_by(year, month, weekdays) |>
  summarize(
    median_duration = median(duration),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

median_duration_df

median_duration_df |>
  ggplot(
    aes(
      x = weekdays,
      y = median_duration,
      color = factor(year),
      group = year
    )
  ) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  facet_grid(. ~ month) +
  labs(
    title = "Median Ride Duration by Weekday",
    x = "Day of the Week",
    y = "Median Ride Duration (minutes)",
    color = "Year"
  ) +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(
      angle = 45,
      hjust = 1
    )
  )
```

Median ride durations were generally longer in July than in January and consistently shorter in 2024 than in 2020. Weekend rides tended to last longer than weekday rides, especially in July 2020, when weekend medians reached approximately 16.5 minutes. These patterns suggest that seasonal conditions and differences between weekday commuting and weekend recreational use may influence ride duration.

### Ride duration by membership and bike type in 2024

```{r}
citibike |>
  filter(year == 2024) |>
  ggplot(
    aes(
      x = rideable_type,
      y = duration,
      fill = member_casual
    )
  ) +
  geom_boxplot(
    alpha = 0.7,
    outlier.alpha = 0.1
  ) +
  facet_grid(. ~ month) +
  scale_y_log10(
    breaks = c(1, 2, 5, 10, 20, 60, 120, 240)
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of Ride Duration in 2024",
    x = "Bike Type",
    y = "Ride Duration (minutes, log scale)",
    fill = "Membership"
  )
```

```{r}
duration_summary =
  citibike |>
  filter(year == 2024) |>
  group_by(
    month, member_casual, rideable_type
  ) |>
  summarize(
    median_duration = median(duration),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

duration_summary |>
  knitr::kable(
    digits = 2,
    caption = "Median Ride Duration by Month, Membership, and Bike Type"
  )
```

Casual riders generally had longer ride durations than members across both months and bike types. In July, casual riders had median durations of 15.62 minutes on classic bikes and 12.94 minutes on electric bikes, compared with 7.68 and 9.24 minutes for members. Ride durations were generally longer in July than January, and casual riders showed greater variability. Among members, electric bike rides tended to be slightly longer than classic bike rides.
